explanations.explanation: That's the opening line. The LORD says, “I have heard your prayer…” (2 Chronicles 7:12). Solomon, Israel's king, had prayed at the temple, and the first thing he hears is that he was heard. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, friend, so I can tell you that hits different.

Gold is a fair guess for a king who just built a temple and a palace. But the LORD never mentions it here. He opens with “I have heard your prayer…” (2 Chronicles 7:12). Most of us would walk in saying, "Nice place!" and the LORD starts with something bigger.

The LORD doesn't say a word about counting anything. His first words to Solomon, Israel's king, are “I have heard your prayer…” (2 Chronicles 7:12). Sacrifice does come up in the very same sentence, but as the kind of house He has chosen. So no tally sheet, just a prayer that was heard.

Yes, sacrifice. The LORD says, “…have chosen this place for Myself as a house of sacrifice.” That's how He describes the temple Solomon built. It's the LORD who says He chose it, and that's what makes this place so special.

I see why a king and a building project make that tempting. But the LORD doesn't call this a house of kings. He says He has chosen this place “…as a house of sacrifice.” The palace is Solomon's own project, and the temple is the one the LORD names for Himself.

Treasure sounds right for a building that big, friend. I'd have guessed it too, and then I'd have tried to stamp it on a cookie. But the LORD says He has chosen this place “…as a house of sacrifice.” Not a vault, not a showroom. A house where sacrifice is offered, and that's the label He gives it.

That's the heart of it. The LORD says, “…if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven…” The hard days could be no rain, locusts or a plague, and the answer is the same: come to Him. I find humbling myself is easy right up until I have to do it.

explanations.answer: Offer more sacrifices at the temple
explanations.explanation: Sacrifice is on the LORD's mind, since He calls the temple a house of sacrifice. But the list in verse 14 doesn't include offering more of them. What He names is that His people humble themselves, pray, seek His face and turn from their wicked ways. Notice there's nothing on that list you can carry in your hands.

explanations.answer: Call on their king for help
explanations.explanation: Reaching out for help is a natural instinct. It's the same one that makes you text the group chat before you read the instructions. But the LORD never says to call on the king. The people He speaks of are the ones called by His name, and they humble themselves, pray, seek His face and turn from their wicked ways (2 Chronicles 7:14).

Heal is right. The LORD says, “…then I will hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.” That's three promises in one sentence. He has just talked about the sky closing, locusts or a plague, so I think a land in trouble would be glad to hear it (2 Chronicles 7:13).

A land in trouble needs a hug, not a flood, friend. The LORD says He will “…hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.” Healing is the word He uses. And the hard times before it, no rain, locusts or a plague, are things He says might come (2 Chronicles 7:13).
Nothing in this promise is about dividing anything. The LORD says He will “…hear from heaven, forgive their sin, and heal their land.” He starts by hearing, then forgiving, then healing.

True. The LORD says, “My eyes and My heart will be there for all time.” He also says He has chosen and consecrated this temple so that His Name may be there forever (2 Chronicles 7:16). Solomon, Israel's king, heard this at night, once the temple and palace were finished. That's a promise worth hearing twice.

The text says the opposite. The LORD tells Solomon, Israel's king, “My eyes and My heart will be there for all time.” (2 Chronicles 7:16). Just before that, He says He has chosen and consecrated this temple so that His Name may be there forever. It's easy to skim past a line like that, friend, so no worries.

Throne it is. The LORD says, “…then I will establish your royal throne, as I covenanted with your father David…” David was Solomon's father and king of Israel before him (1 Kings 2:12). The promise comes with a condition: Solomon walks before the LORD as David walked. I bet that's a lot of pressure for one man.

An army is a natural thing to picture for a king, and it would look great on a cookie. But the LORD never mentions one here. He says, “…then I will establish your royal throne…” (2 Chronicles 7:18). The promise is about the seat of the king himself, tied to the covenant with his father David, so that's the word for the blank.

Solomon, Israel's king, had just built a temple and a palace, so a treasury feels close. But the LORD doesn't say it. He says, “…then I will establish your royal throne…” (2 Chronicles 7:18). It's a promise about his throne, tied to the covenant with his father David.

Right. The LORD warns, “But if you turn away and forsake the statutes and commandments I have set before you, and if you go off to serve and worship other gods…” (2 Chronicles 7:19). Turning away from His commands and going off to other gods are put right next to each other. It's the other side of the promise to Solomon, Israel's king.

Treaties are a reasonable guess, but they're not in this warning. The LORD says, “…if you go off to serve and worship other gods…” (2 Chronicles 7:19). That's the thing He names after turning away from His statutes and commandments.

explanations.answer: Build altars on the high hills
explanations.explanation: Altars on hills sound like a detail that could fit, friend. But the LORD doesn't mention them in this warning. He says, “…if you go off to serve and worship other gods…” (2 Chronicles 7:19). That's what He warns about here.

That's what He says. “…then I will uproot Israel from the soil I have given them…” (2 Chronicles 7:20). I think this is a heavy part, friend. Still, it comes with a clear warning, spoken to Solomon, Israel's king, ahead of time.

Egypt does come up later in the passage, but not as a place to go back to. It's named as where the LORD brought their fathers out of (2 Chronicles 7:22). The warning itself says, “…I will uproot Israel from the soil I have given them…” (2 Chronicles 7:20). That's a heavy line, and it's about the land.

The warning doesn't name the king. The LORD says, “…then I will uproot Israel from the soil I have given them…” (2 Chronicles 7:20). It's about the land He gave them. I think this is a heavy word, so it's worth reading slowly.

The text says the opposite. The LORD says, “And when this temple has become a heap of rubble, all who pass by it will be appalled and say, ‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land and to this temple?’” (2 Chronicles 7:21). They'd be appalled, and they'd ask about it. I think this is one of the heavy lines in the passage.

False is right. The LORD says all who pass by will be “appalled” and will ask, “…‘Why has the LORD done such a thing to this land and to this temple?’” (2 Chronicles 7:21). Nobody walks by without noticing. I think that's a heavy picture, friend.
